newsitem.title: USA: Las Cruces to stay with El Paso Electric until Jan.
newsitem.headline: Las Cruces to stay with El Paso Electric until Jan.

text.p: The city of Las Cruces, New Mexico, will continue to purchase its power from El Paso Electric Co until January, when a new substation is expected to be ready, a spokesman for the city said Wednesday.
"We will continue to be captive to their incredibly high rates," spokesman Christopher Good said.

Earlier in the day, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) ordered El Paso to respond within 30 days to a long-standing request by Southwestern Public Service Co for access to El Paso's transmission system.
Las Cruces chose SPS to replace El Paso as the city's power supplier more than two years ago after SPS guaranteed a 20 percent reduction in electricity rates.
Las Cruces has sought since the early 1990's to form its own municipal utility through the acquistion of El Paso's distribution system.
But El Paso has fought to keep Las Cruces as part of its retail service territory, unless it can get compensation for "stranded costs" attributable to the New Mexico town.
El Paso calculates costs associated with its Las Cruces distribution system at $234 million, compared with appraisals by others as low as $38 million.
Las Cruces decided earlier this year to go ahead with construction of the new substation, which will serve an industrial park, despite the lack of incoming transmission access.
Las Cruces' city council has said it would not pay more than $90 million for the existing transmission and distribution assets, Good noted.
Also on Wednesday, FERC declined to rule on the stranded costs issue, setting instead plans for a separate hearing on the dispute.
In a 1996 order, FERC required utilities to open their transmission systems to competition, while allowing the companies to recover investments made under the traditional regulatory system.
But Las Cruces maintains El Paso "had no reasonable expectation to continue serving the city" since the late 1980's, when Las Cruces made its intentions clear, Good said.
The city voted formally to switch to Southwestern Power in 1994.
